title: 11 — Single-Node Engines
html:
11 — Single-Node Engines

The one idea: most tables in a financial platform fit on one large machine. A modern single-node engine (Polars, DuckDB, Daft) reading open Parquet and Iceberg through a catalog is often faster and far cheaper than a cluster. Use Spark when the data or the shuffle truly needs many machines.

1. What it is

Engine What it is Interface Iceberg (checked 2026-10-26)
Polars DataFrame library in Rust, with lazy queries and a streaming engine Python expressions Native Iceberg reader, and an Iceberg sink for the streaming engine (2026). Polars Cloud adds a distributed engine, with a distributed Iceberg sink in release 0.6.3
DuckDB In-process analytical SQL database SQL, Python, many languages iceberg extension: reads, plus writes through a REST catalog (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE INTO per current docs). Writes must go through a catalog. Earlier versions could not update partitioned or sorted tables
DuckLake A lakehouse format from the DuckDB team: metadata in a SQL database, data in Parquet SQL Its own format, not Iceberg. v1.0 (production-ready, backward-compatible) shipped with DuckDB 1.5.2 in April 2026
Daft Distributed DataFrame engine for AI and multimodal data, with a native local runner Python, SQL Reads and writes Iceberg, Delta, Hudi and (from v0.7.6, March 2026) Paimon. Works with Unity Catalog
PyIceberg The Python implementation of Iceberg Python Catalogs, scans, appends, overwrites. Pairs with any Arrow engine. A Rust core (pyiceberg-core, from iceberg-rust) speeds up parts of it

Spark comparison: Spark spreads work across a cluster, so it pays scheduling and shuffle costs that a single process never pays.

2. Why it matters

  • Cost and speed: most daily batches in a fund-data platform are gigabytes, not terabytes.
  • Openness: if your tables are Iceberg in your own storage, every one of these engines can read them, and Databricks is one engine among several.
  • Developer loop: run the same pipeline code on a laptop, in CI, and in production.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Choosing

---
title: Choosing an engine for a job
---
flowchart TD
    Q["New job"] --> SIZE{"Working set fits on one<br/>large machine (with streaming)?"}
    SIZE -- "no" --> SPARK["Spark / Databricks SQL<br/>(distributed)"]
    SIZE -- "yes" --> KIND{"Mostly SQL, joins,<br/>ad-hoc analysis?"}
    KIND -- "yes" --> DUCK["DuckDB"]
    KIND -- "no" --> MM{"Images, documents,<br/>model calls per row?"}
    MM -- "yes" --> DAFT["Daft"]
    MM -- "no" --> POLARS["Polars (lazy + streaming)"]
    DUCK --> IO["Read and write Iceberg<br/>through PyIceberg or a REST catalog"]
    POLARS --> IO
    DAFT --> IO

3.2 Lazy execution, again

Polars LazyFrame and DuckDB both build a query plan first and optimise it: they push filters down into the Parquet reader, prune columns, and reorder joins. The .NET comparison is IQueryable<T> building an expression tree before EF Core translates it. Always start from scan_* (lazy), not read_* (eager), for large inputs.

3.3 Streaming execution

Both Polars (with collect(engine="streaming")) and DuckDB process data in batches, so inputs larger than memory still run. Spilling and streaming support differs by operation, so profile heavy joins.

4. Working code

These examples are not run: Polars, DuckDB, Daft and PyIceberg could not be installed in the build environment (no package registry access). They use documented public APIs, but check the docs for your installed versions, because these libraries change quickly.

# Not run. Polars: lazy scan, filter pushdown, aggregate, then write back as Iceberg.
import polars as pl
from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog

catalog = SqlCatalog("local", uri="sqlite:///catalog.db", warehouse="file:///tmp/warehouse")
nav = catalog.load_table("fin.nav")

summary = (pl.scan_iceberg(nav)
             .filter(pl.col("nav_date") >= "2026-10-01")
             .group_by("isin")
             .agg(pl.col("nav").last().alias("last_nav"), pl.len().alias("days"))
             .collect(engine="streaming"))

summary.write_iceberg(catalog.load_table("fin.nav_month_summary"), mode="append")

-- Not run. DuckDB with the iceberg extension against a REST catalog.
-- The ATTACH options and secret syntax depend on the catalog. See DuckDB's Iceberg docs.
INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
ATTACH 'fin_warehouse' AS ice (TYPE iceberg, ENDPOINT 'https://catalog.example.com/api');
SELECT isin, max(nav_date) AS latest FROM ice.fin.nav GROUP BY isin;
MERGE INTO ice.fin.fund_master t USING staged s ON t.isin = s.isin
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = s.name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

-- DuckLake: metadata in a database file, data in Parquet.
INSTALL ducklake; LOAD ducklake;
ATTACH 'ducklake:metadata.ducklake' AS lake (DATA_PATH 'lake_data/');

# Not run. Daft: read an Iceberg table and run a per-row function, then write Iceberg.
import daft
df = daft.read_iceberg(nav)                       # nav: the PyIceberg table from above
df = df.where(df["nav"] > 0).with_column("nav_x100", df["nav"] * 100)
df.write_iceberg(catalog.load_table("fin.nav_scaled"), mode="append")

5. Common mistakes

  1. Eager reads of big files. read_parquet loads everything. scan_parquet lets the optimiser prune.
  2. Writing Iceberg by dropping Parquet files into the folder. Always commit through a catalog (PyIceberg, a REST catalog, or the engine's integration).
  3. Converting through pandas. You lose zero-copy and types. Stay in Arrow between engines.
  4. Assuming every engine supports every Iceberg feature. Check v3, deletion vectors and partitioned writes per engine and version.
  5. Choosing a cluster by habit. Measure on one machine first.

6. Exercise (2 hours, on a laptop)

  1. Install PyIceberg, Polars and DuckDB. Create a SQLite-backed catalog and a NAV table. Append 30 days of made-up data.
  2. Run the same "last NAV per ISIN" query in Polars and DuckDB, and compare the timings.
  3. Make a correction by appending a new version row (never updating in place), and query it as of two dates using a knowledge-time column.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. When is Spark the right choice over a single-node engine?
  2. What does lazy execution let the engine do?
  3. What must DuckDB writes to Iceberg go through?
  4. What is DuckLake, and how is it different from Iceberg?
  5. Which engine fits per-row model calls on documents?

Answers

  1. When the working set or the shuffle won't fit on one large machine, even with streaming.
  2. Optimise the whole plan: push filters and column selection into the reader, reorder joins, and skip unneeded data.
  3. An attached catalog. Tables read directly from storage with iceberg_scan can't be written.
  4. A lakehouse format whose metadata lives in a SQL database rather than in metadata files. It is a separate format, with v1.0 released in April 2026.
  5. Daft, which is built for multimodal and AI workloads.
